t.2.61.1: When the night had passed and the sun had risen, the twice-born king-makers then assembled together and went to the hall of council.
t.2.61.2: Then came Mārkaṇḍeya, Maudgalya, Vāmadeva and Kāśyapa, Kātyāyana and Gautama, and the greatly renowned Jābāli.
t.2.61.3: These twice-born, together with the ministers, each spoke out separately, facing Vasiṣṭha alone, the foremost royal priest.
t.2.61.4: Painfully has the night passed, which was for us like a hundred years, now that this king has gone to his death through grief for his son.
t.2.61.5: The great king has gone to heaven, Rāma has taken refuge in the forest, and the splendid Lakṣmaṇa too has gone away together with Rāma himself.
t.2.61.6: Both Bharata and Śatrughna, the scorchers of foes, are among the Kekayas, in the delightful city of Rājagṛha, in the residence of their maternal grandfather.
t.2.61.7: Let someone of the Ikṣvākus be appointed king here this very day, so that our kingdom, left without a king, may not meet with destruction.
t.2.61.8: In a land without a king, the rain-cloud, garlanded with lightning and loudly thundering, does not shower the earth with heavenly water.
t.2.61.9: In a kingless land not even a handful of seed is scattered; in a kingless land the son does not remain under his father's control, nor the wife under her husband's.
t.2.61.10: In a kingless land there is no wealth, and in a kingless land there is no wife either. This is another great calamity: how can there be truth in a kingless land?
t.2.61.11: In a land without a king, men do not joyfully build assembly halls, nor delightful gardens, nor sacred houses.
t.2.61.12: In a land without a king, the twice-born, devoted to sacrifice, do not attend the sacrificial sessions, nor do self-controlled brāhmaṇas firm in their vows.
t.2.61.13: In a kingless land, festivals and assemblies, abounding in actors and dancers, which make the kingdom prosper, do not flourish.
t.2.61.15: In a land without a king, men in love do not drive out to the forests with their women on swift-moving vehicles.
t.2.61.14: In a kingless land, merchants who have accomplished their aims, given as they are to conversation, do not delight in tales together with those who love tales.
t.2.61.16: In a land without a king, the wealthy who live by farming and tending cattle do not sleep well protected, with their doors left open.
t.2.61.17: In a kingless land, merchants who travel far, laden with abundant goods, cannot journey along a safe road.
t.2.61.18: In a kingless land no self-controlled sage wanders alone, contemplating the self by the self, making his home wherever evening finds him.
t.2.61.19: In a kingless land, the securing of new gains and the safeguarding of what is held does not go on; nor, in a kingless land, can the army withstand its enemies in battle.
t.2.61.20: As rivers without water, as a forest without grass, as cows without a herdsman, so is a kingdom without a king.
t.2.61.21: In a kingless land nothing belongs to anyone as his own; like fish, men constantly devour one another.
t.2.61.22: For even those who have broken through the bounds of propriety, unbelievers free of all scruple, become fit for right conduct when they are crushed by the king's punishment.
t.2.61.23: Alas, this world would be as if plunged in darkness, and nothing at all would be discerned, if there were no king in the world to distinguish between good and evil.
t.2.61.24: Even while the great king is still living, all of us do not transgress your word alone, just as the ocean, having reached its shore, does not pass beyond it.
t.2.61.25: Considering us, and the kingdom, which without a king has become a wilderness, you yourself must consecrate here as king a generous prince, a son of Ikṣvāku, whose conduct is like that of the best of the twice-born.
